Jean-Jacques Rousseau. A Genevan philosopher whose radical challenge to rationalism and emphasis on natural feeling, popular sovereignty, and collective will shaped Enlightenment thought and the ideological foundations of revolution. Through works like The Social Contract and Emile, he argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed and that human nature is naturally good but corrupted by civilization. His ideas profoundly influenced the French Revolution and modern democratic theory, though his philosophy remains deeply contested. Rousseau was born in Geneva in seventeen twelve and spent formative years as a wanderer, musician, and household tutor across Europe. He published Discourse on Inequality in seventeen fifty-five, arguing that private property and social hierarchy corrupted natural human equality. He wrote The Social Contract in seventeen sixty-two, proposing that legitimate government derives from a social contract between free individuals and that the "general will" supersedes individual rights. In Emile, also published in seventeen sixty-two, he argued that education should nurture natural human development rather than impose conformity. Children learn through experience and feeling. His ideas on nature and natural feeling rejected Cartesian rationalism, elevating emotion and intuition as valid paths to knowledge. Rousseau fled France and Switzerland as his writings drew condemnation from authorities. He died in exile in Paris in seventeen seventy-eight. His vision of popular sovereignty and the general will became foundational to modern political thought and revolutionary ideology.
